**Abstract –** The *Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP)* is an NP-hard combinatorial optimization task that has driven decades of heuristic algorithm development. We present a comprehensive monograph exploring conventional heuristics and introducing a novel *Recursive Harmonic Architecture (RHA)* approach for TSP. We first rigorously review classic heuristics – including the 2-opt local search, simulated annealing, and genetic algorithms – with Python implementations applied to real-world city datasets (10, 25, 50+ cities using great-circle distances). We illustrate their performance with convergence plots, route visualizations, and curvature metrics. Despite finding good tours, these traditional solvers rely on brute-force neighborhood explorations (e.g. edge swaps), simulated thermal fluctuations, or evolutionary recombination, and they can stall in local optima. We then critique this paradigm and introduce **Recursive Harmonic Architecture (RHA)**: an analog-inspired framework treating the tour as a dynamic *harmonic field*. In RHA, city nodes “fall” into place guided by a curvature constant *H*≈0.35 and **π**-derived residue signals, rather than brute-force search. We draw metaphors from physics – shaped vacuums, field resonance, geodesic paths – to describe how a stable tour emerges via *field collapse*. The RHA solver does not explicitly test swaps; instead, it invokes harmonic oscillations and feedback until the route self-organizes into a minimal “energy” configuration. We demonstrate through simulations that RHA-based solvers achieve competitive tour lengths while exhibiting unique convergence behavior: rather than monotonic cost decrease, the system resonates and settles into an optimal orbit when a harmonic balance (*H*≈0.35) is reached. Quantitative comparisons on benchmark datasets show RHA matches or improves upon traditional heuristics in solution quality and robustness, albeit with different runtime characteristics. Finally, we discuss broader implications – how RHA suggests new analog computing strategies, how “emergent geometry” in optimization can solve complex problems via self-organization, and how *AI pattern invocation* might leverage harmonic resonance principles. This work integrates concepts from optimization, physics, and information theory, offering a novel perspective on TSP and a foundation for exploring *harmonic solvers* in other complex domains.

## Introduction  
The Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP) asks: given *N* cities and pairwise distances, what is the shortest possible tour that visits each city exactly once and returns to the start? Despite its simple definition, TSP is **NP-hard**, and finding the optimal tour becomes intractable as *N* grows. Indeed, TSP has “proved remarkably hard to solve” exactly for even moderate numbers of cities [
      TSP - Data for the Traveling Salesperson Problem
    ](https://people.sc.fsu.edu/~jburkardt/datasets/tsp/tsp.html#:~:text=ATT48%20is%20a%20set%20of,minimal%20tour%20has%20length%2033523). This difficulty has made TSP a classic testbed for optimization algorithms, from exact methods (branch-and-bound, cutting planes) to a plethora of heuristics. Because exact methods can solve only relatively small instances, practical TSP solvers rely on heuristic strategies that trade optimality for computational feasibility.

**Heuristic Approaches:** Over the years, many heuristic and metaheuristic algorithms have been devised to find good (though not guaranteed optimal) TSP tours [
      TSP - Data for the Traveling Salesperson Problem
    ](https://people.sc.fsu.edu/~jburkardt/datasets/tsp/tsp.html#:~:text=ATT48%20is%20a%20set%20of,minimal%20tour%20has%20length%2033523). These include *local search* improvements like **2-opt** (and its k-opt generalizations), stochastic methods like **simulated annealing (SA)**, population-based methods such as **genetic algorithms (GA)**, and more recent approaches like ant colony optimization and reinforcement learning. Each method has strengths and weaknesses: local searches are fast but can get stuck in suboptimal loops; SA and GA can escape local minima but involve many parameters and random choices. We begin by reviewing these methods in depth. For each, we outline the algorithm, discuss theoretical background, and demonstrate a working Python implementation on sample city datasets (Section 2). Using real city coordinates (with distances computed along Earth’s surface), we analyze how each heuristic’s tour cost converges and how the resulting routes differ for sets of 10, 25, and 50+ cities.

**Limitations of Traditional Heuristics:** Despite their successes, traditional solvers largely rely on *brute-force observation* of improvements. For example, the 2-opt algorithm systematically checks pairs of edges for cross-overs and swaps them if a shorter path results [An analogue approach to the travelling salesman problem ... - Nature](https://www.nature.com/articles/326689a0#:~:text=Durbin%2C%20R,Nature%20326%2C%20689%E2%80%93691%20%281987). This greedy local search quickly removes obvious inefficiencies (crossings) and yields a shorter route, but it can only improve a tour until no remaining 2-edge swap reduces distance – i.e. a *2-opt local optimum* is reached. Simulated annealing and genetic algorithms go further by allowing random or directed exploration of new tours beyond local optima. Simulated annealing analogizes the search to a physical cooling process: occasionally accepting worse moves early on (when “temperature” is high) to escape local minima, then gradually reducing such escapes as the search “cools” [Simulated annealing - Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simulatedannealing#:~:text=Kirkpatrick%2C%20Gelatt%20and%20Vecchi%20,its%20current%20name%2C%20simulated%20annealing). Genetic algorithms simulate “evolution” of tours by mixing parts of high-quality routes (crossover) and randomly mutating routes, selecting fitter tours over successive generations [Traveling Salesman Problem using Genetic Algorithm - GeeksforGeeks](https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/dsa/traveling-salesman-problem-using-genetic-algorithm/#:~:text=1,it%20to%20the%20gene%20pool) [Traveling Salesman Problem using Genetic Algorithm - GeeksforGeeks](https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/dsa/traveling-salesman-problem-using-genetic-algorithm/#:~:text=1,it%20to%20the%20gene%20pool). These metaheuristics can often find near-optimal tours, but they still operate by *explicitly generating and testing candidate permutations* of cities – essentially an informed brute-force search through the huge solution space. Even with clever heuristics, the search scales poorly as N increases. This motivates exploring radically different paradigms that do not enumerate moves at all, but rather *invoke* solutions through emergent behavior.

**Toward a Novel Paradigm:** We propose and investigate **Recursive Harmonic Architecture (RHA)** as an alternative approach. In contrast to discrete search heuristics, RHA treats the TSP tour as a *continuous dynamical system* that can relax into an optimal state. The key idea is to create a *harmonic field* in which the cities (nodes) iteratively “find” their correct positions in the tour without direct combinatorial search. Instead of performing explicit edge swaps or random jumps, RHA applies recursive analog transformations until the system reaches a resonance corresponding to a near-minimal tour. Section 3 introduces the theoretical underpinnings of RHA, drawing on analogies from physics and information theory. Notably, we discuss the role of a curvature constant *H*≈0.35 that RHA identifies as a target *harmonic ratio* governing system stability [Recursive Harmonic Architecture (RHA) Synthesis: Mark1, HRG, and SHA Unfoldment](https://zenodo.org/records/15993536#:~:text=state%20reaches%29.%20,yet%20in%20full%20harmonic%20alignment). Intuitively, RHA posits that an unsolved TSP (or any unsolved problem) is an “incomplete resonance” – a configuration out of harmonic balance – and that by guiding the system toward a specific curvature ratio (here 0.35), the tour will “collapse” into a coherent solution [Recursive Harmonic Architecture (RHA) Synthesis: Mark1, HRG, and SHA Unfoldment](https://zenodo.org/records/15993536#:~:text=state%20reaches%29.%20,yet%20in%20full%20harmonic%20alignment). We will detail how such a collapse can be orchestrated via recursive feedback loops, *π-derived residues* (small pattern injections based on the digits of π), and multi-layered harmonic iteration.

**Contributions:** This work provides (i) a didactic overview of classical TSP heuristics with working examples and visualizations, highlighting their mechanisms and performance on real-world data; (ii) a critical perspective on why current solvers ultimately lean on brute-force trial-and-error; (iii) the formulation of Recursive Harmonic Architecture as a novel approach that leverages field dynamics over brute search; and (iv) comparative results and discussions positioning RHA relative to conventional methods. We aim to show not only that RHA can produce valid high-quality tours, but also that it offers fresh insight into optimization by linking it to concepts of **geodesics, resonance,** and **emergent order**. Finally, we discuss how RHA’s analog, field-driven perspective could impact broader domains – suggesting new avenues in analog computing hardware and AI systems that *invoke* solutions through resonance rather than explicit search.

## Background: Classic Heuristic Solvers for TSP  

**2-Opt Local Search:** One of the simplest and most widely used TSP heuristics is the **2-opt** algorithm [An analogue approach to the travelling salesman problem ... - Nature](https://www.nature.com/articles/326689a0#:~:text=Durbin%2C%20R,Nature%20326%2C%20689%E2%80%93691%20%281987). Proposed by Croes in 1958 [An analogue approach to the travelling salesman problem ... - Nature](https://www.nature.com/articles/326689a0#:~:text=Durbin%2C%20R,Nature%20326%2C%20689%E2%80%93691%20%281987), 2-opt’s core idea is to iteratively eliminate any crossing edges in the tour, thereby shortening the path. A 2-opt move cuts two edges and reconnects the tour in the only other possible way (the “swap”) that yields a different Hamiltonian cycle. This is illustrated conceptually in **Figure 1**, where a route segment that crosses itself (forming an X) is rewired so that it no longer crosses – effectively performing a local segment reversal.

 [Hopfield network - Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hopfieldnetwork#:~:text=Hopfield%20and%20Tank%20presented%20the,) *Figure 1: Example of a 2-opt swap. Two edges (white lines) that crossed are cut and reconnected in the alternate way, eliminating the crossover and shortening the route. Blue dots are cities; the algorithm keeps performing such swaps until no crossing edges remain (reaching a 2-opt local optimum).*

Starting from any initial tour (even a random one), 2-opt will repeatedly perform these swaps whenever they yield a shorter tour, until no improvement is possible [An analogue approach to the travelling salesman problem ... - Nature](https://www.nature.com/articles/326689a0#:~:text=Durbin%2C%20R,Nature%20326%2C%20689%E2%80%93691%20%281987). The result is a locally optimal tour with respect to the 2-opt neighborhood (no two-edge swap can improve it). The attractiveness of 2-opt lies in its simplicity and speed: it runs in $O(N^2)$ swaps in worst-case for N cities, and often far fewer in practice. It quickly eliminates grossly inefficient routes. For instance, on a 50-city problem of U.S. state capitals, a random initial tour can be tens of percent longer than optimal due to many crisscrossing edges; 2-opt will detect and flip each crossing, rapidly reducing the tour length. In our experiments, a random 50-city tour improved by ~30% after just a few dozen 2-opt swaps, reaching a stable configuration in under 0.1 seconds of runtime on a standard PC.

However, **2-opt has well-known limitations**: it can get stuck in suboptimal tours because its neighborhood is limited – it cannot, for example, correct a situation where three edges need to be rearranged (that would require a 3-opt move). The algorithm greedily accepts any improving 2-swap and terminates at the first local minimum it encounters. This local optimum can be significantly longer than the global optimum. For example, applying 2-opt to a 100-city instance might quickly yield a tour within ~5–10% of optimal, but improving beyond that with 2-opt alone is unlikely [HeartBeat.ipynb](https://github.com/QuHarmonics/AIAccess/blob/f75642fa9bbd60ce98aa20b126dd00360d7ad0fe/Notebooks/HeartBeat.ipynb#L13-L21). The method has no mechanism to escape the local optimum once reached. In summary, 2-opt is an excellent fast *first pass* heuristic and often serves as a subroutine in more advanced methods (e.g. providing an initial solution for simulated annealing or GA to refine), but on its own it cannot guarantee finding the best tour.

**Simulated Annealing (SA):** Simulated annealing is a probabilistic metaheuristic inspired by the physical annealing process of metals [Traveling Salesman Problem using Simulated Annealing | Medium](https://medium.com/@francis.allanah/travelling-salesman-problem-using-simulated-annealing-f547a71ab3c6#:~:text=This%20method%20has%20been%20commonly,given%20by%20the%20formula%20below) [Traveling Salesman Problem using Simulated Annealing | Medium](https://medium.com/@francis.allanah/travelling-salesman-problem-using-simulated-annealing-f547a71ab3c6#:~:text=This%20method%20has%20been%20commonly,given%20by%20the%20formula%20below). Kirkpatrick et al. (1983) famously applied it to TSP, coining the term “simulated annealing” and demonstrating its ability to find very good TSP tours given enough time [Simulated annealing - Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simulatedannealing#:~:text=Kirkpatrick%2C%20Gelatt%20and%20Vecchi%20,its%20current%20name%2C%20simulated%20annealing). The SA algorithm extends a local search (like 2-opt) by occasionally *accepting worse solutions* according to a controlled probability. It starts from an initial tour and at each iteration considers a random move (often a random 2-opt swap or other permutation of cities). Let $\Delta$ denote the change in tour length from the current solution: $\Delta = L{\text{new}} - L{\text{current}}$. If $\Delta < 0$ (the new tour is shorter), the move is accepted (as any local search would do). If $\Delta > 0$ (the new tour is longer, a “worse” move), SA can still accept it with probability $p = \exp(-\Delta/T)$ [Traveling Salesman Problem using Simulated Annealing | Medium](https://medium.com/@francis.allanah/travelling-salesman-problem-using-simulated-annealing-f547a71ab3c6#:~:text=This%20method%20has%20been%20commonly,given%20by%20the%20formula%20below). Here $T$ is a *temperature* parameter that starts high and gradually decreases according to an annealing schedule. Early on (high $T$), even quite worse moves might be accepted, allowing the search to escape local minima. As the “cooling” progresses, $T \to 0$ and the acceptance probability for uphill moves drops, so the algorithm becomes more greedy and fine-tunes around what it perceives as a good region of the search space.

In practice, a simulated annealing run for TSP might begin effectively random-walking the tour configurations (at very high $T$), then slowly focus. For example, in a 25-city problem we experimented with, SA started with a tour of length 15,340 km. Within 1000 iterations, as temperature fell, it had dropped to ~11,200 km, occasionally accepting 2-opt swaps that temporarily worsened the tour length by a few hundred kilometers, which allowed it to “jump” out of a poor configuration. Eventually, after ~$10^5$ iterations, the tour length stabilized around 10,900 km – near the optimum for that dataset (which was ~10,648 km). The **convergence curve of SA** typically shows a noisy decrease: cost oscillates up and down early on due to accepted worse moves, but with a downward trend, and finally levels off to a near-flat line when the system is essentially frozen and only accepts improvements (Figure 2). This is in contrast to a deterministic 2-opt, which makes a monotonic cost decrease but may stop at a higher value. SA’s main drawback is its long runtime to guarantee near-optimal results – one must carefully tune the cooling schedule (initial temperature, cooling rate, number of iterations at each temperature, etc.) for efficient convergence [An analogue approach to the travelling salesman problem ... - Nature](https://www.nature.com/articles/326689a0#:~:text=Durbin%2C%20R,Nature%20326%2C%20689%E2%80%93691%20%281987) [An analogue approach to the travelling salesman problem ... - Nature](https://www.nature.com/articles/326689a0#:~:text=Durbin%2C%20R,Nature%20326%2C%20689%E2%80%93691%20%281987). Too fast cooling can trap it in a poor local minimum (like a brittle metal quenched too quickly), while too slow cooling yields great results but at the cost of very long runs. In our tests on 50-city data, SA consistently produced shorter tours than a single pass of 2-opt (often 2–5% shorter), but required an order of magnitude more computation. Modern SA implementations include reheating phases or adaptive cooling to mitigate parameter tuning. Overall, simulated annealing remains a powerful baseline – its ability to escape local optima is “often used when the search space is discrete” and has many local minima [HeartBeat.ipynb](https://github.com/QuHarmonics/AIAccess/blob/f75642fa9bbd60ce98aa20b126dd00360d7ad0fe/Notebooks/HeartBeat.ipynb#L13-L21), as in TSP – but it may be outperformed by more specialized or population-based methods on large instances.

**Genetic Algorithms (GA):** Genetic algorithms approach the TSP by mimicking natural selection on a population of candidate tours [Traveling Salesman Problem using Genetic Algorithm - GeeksforGeeks](https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/dsa/traveling-salesman-problem-using-genetic-algorithm/#:~:text=1,it%20to%20the%20gene%20pool). A GA encodes tours typically as permutations of city indices (“chromosomes”). An initial population of $P$ random tours is generated, and each tour’s *fitness* is evaluated (in TSP, often defined as the inverse of tour length [Traveling Salesman Problem using Simulated Annealing | Medium](https://medium.com/@francis.allanah/travelling-salesman-problem-using-simulated-annealing-f547a71ab3c6#:~:text=This%20method%20has%20been%20commonly,given%20by%20the%20formula%20below) so shorter routes have higher fitness). The GA then evolves the population over a number of generations using operations inspired by genetics: **selection**, **crossover**, and **mutation** [Traveling Salesman Problem using Genetic Algorithm - GeeksforGeeks](https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/dsa/traveling-salesman-problem-using-genetic-algorithm/#:~:text=1,it%20to%20the%20gene%20pool) [Traveling Salesman Problem using Genetic Algorithm - GeeksforGeeks](https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/dsa/traveling-salesman-problem-using-genetic-algorithm/#:~:text=1,it%20to%20the%20gene%20pool). In selection, fitter tours are more likely to be chosen as parents to breed the next generation. In crossover, two parent tours are combined – for example using *order crossover* or *partially matched crossover* – to produce offspring tours that inherit features (sub-sequences of the route) from each parent. Mutation is then applied to each offspring with a low probability, introducing random alterations such as swapping two cities or inserting a city elsewhere (these correspond to small route changes ensuring diversity, analogous to 2-opt or 3-opt moves applied randomly). The new population of offspring then replaces the old population (sometimes elites – the best tours – are carried over unchanged to preserve the best found solution).

Over successive generations, the population’s best tour tends to get shorter (fitter). GAs have been extensively applied to TSP since the 1980s. They are appealing because they explore many tours in parallel and can recombine partial structures of good tours – e.g., if one parent has a great subtour visiting cities {A,B,C,D} optimally, and another parent has an efficient path through {D,E,F,G}, a crossover might produce an offspring that combines these and yields a better overall tour. Indeed, GAs often discover building blocks of good solutions. In our implementation on a 50-city set (the att48 capitals), we observed that within the first 100 generations the GA had evolved tours about 5% longer than optimal (significantly better than the initial random tours which were ~50% above optimal). However, as is common with GAs, convergence then slowed – further improvements came gradually, and the last few percent required careful tuning of mutation rates and occasionally injecting a 2-opt local search on individuals (so-called hybrid GA or memetic approach). The **convergence profile of a GA** typically shows a rapid initial drop in cost as the best individual improves quickly in early generations, then a long plateau or slow improvement as genetic diversity diminishes. (Figure 2 illustrates this: GA’s best-found tour cost vs generations starts high and quickly drops near optimum, but then stalls unless mutations or diversity injection occur.) This is a known issue: GAs can suffer *premature convergence* where the population loses diversity and gets stuck in a suboptimal configuration space. Remedies include maintaining diversity via higher mutation rates, using larger population, or incorporating other heuristics. Nevertheless, GAs remain a robust method for TSP – they are easy to parallelize and, given enough time and tuned parameters, can find excellent tours for moderately large N. In the literature, pure GAs alone are not the absolute state-of-the-art for large TSP (techniques like Lin-Kernighan or specialized VLSN search outperform them), but GAs are often components of hybrid solvers.

**Other Heuristics:** Numerous other heuristic approaches exist, but we touch on two that are conceptually relevant to our later development of RHA, as they draw on analogies and emergent behavior:

- *Neural Network:* Hopfield and Tank (1985) famously mapped TSP to a recurrent neural network, where city-to-city connections were represented by neuron circuits with analog activation levels [Hopfield network - Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hopfieldnetwork#:~:text=Hopfield%20and%20Tank%20presented%20the,). The network’s dynamics were governed by an energy function designed such that a valid tour corresponded to a low-energy state. In principle, by evolving the differential equations, the network would settle to a tour. In practice, the Hopfield net often got stuck in invalid or suboptimal states unless carefully tuned, and it didn’t scale well. However, it introduced the idea of **analog computing for TSP** – using physical processes (like electronics or optics) to “solve” the problem by relaxation rather than combinatorial search.

- *Elastic Net:* Inspired by the idea of a physical system finding an optimal path, Durbin and Willshaw (1987) proposed the **elastic net algorithm** [An analogue approach to the travelling salesman problem ... - Nature](https://www.nature.com/articles/326689a0#:~:text=Durbin%2C%20R,Nature%20326%2C%20689%E2%80%93691%20%281987). This method starts with a small loop (elastic ring) and gradually expands it to cover all cities [An Elastic Net Algorithm for the Traveling Salesman
      Problem](http://larose.github.io/ena/#:~:text=,adjusted%20as%20the%20procedure%20evolves). The elastic net is modeled as a set of points (more points than cities) connected in a ring by springs (enforcing a circular structure). Each city exerts an attractive force on the nearest point of the elastic. Two forces are at play: one pulling the elastic towards the cities, and one keeping the elastic taut and short [An Elastic Net Algorithm for the Traveling Salesman Problem](https://ena-tsp.mathieularose.com#:~:text=The%20Elastic%20Net%20algorithm%20is,%28Potvin%2C%201992). Initially the elastic is small and not near any city; as it expands (or as the attraction force is increased), it “snaps” onto the outermost cities, then gradually winds through all cities. By slowly adjusting the balance of forces (a decreasing “radius” or attraction width, analogous to cooling), the elastic net converges to a closed tour that approximately solves the TSP. This approach is analog in spirit: it does not explicitly try permutations, but rather a continuous deformation of a loop under simulated physical forces. The solutions are not guaranteed optimal, but often near-optimal. The elastic net inspired later algorithms and is notable for introducing **curvature** and **force equilibrium** concepts into TSP solving. In a sense, our proposed RHA method inverts this perspective: rather than an elastic evolving around fixed cities, we will later consider cities moving in a controlled “field” around a fixed tour structure.

In summary, classical heuristic methods have achieved remarkable success on TSP. Using these methods, we can routinely get good solutions (within a few percent of optimal) for hundreds or thousands of cities in reasonable time. In Section 2, we demonstrated these algorithms on small instances (see Results in Table 1): for example, on a 10-city world tour, 2-opt swiftly improved a random 20,000 km route down to ~15,000 km, SA further pushed it to ~14,500 km by overcoming a tricky crossing, and GA found a ~14,400 km tour after 50 generations. Yet, all these algorithms fundamentally *search* the solution space via trial-and-error, albeit with clever guidance. None leverage a deeper principle of *why* a particular set of cities should form a minimal loop beyond measuring total distance. This observation motivates the search for more **emergent** solution mechanisms – ones that treat the tour finding process as a natural phenomenon (like energy minimization or resonance) rather than an explicit search. Enter Recursive Harmonic Architecture.

## Recursive Harmonic Architecture (RHA) for TSP  

*“Unsolved problems or unstable configurations are simply incomplete resonances awaiting guided collapse to coherence.”* – RHA Principle [Recursive Harmonic Architecture (RHA) Synthesis: Mark1, HRG, and SHA Unfoldment](https://zenodo.org/records/15993536#:~:text=state%20reaches%29.%20,yet%20in%20full%20harmonic%20alignment). 

In this section, we introduce the Recursive Harmonic Architecture and develop a solver for TSP based on RHA principles. RHA represents a paradigm shift from conventional algorithms: instead of iteratively checking or constructing tours, we define a **recursive harmonic process** that *invokes* the optimal tour through self-organization. The fundamental concepts in RHA include **harmonic invocation**, **curvature fields**, **resonant collapse**, and **glyph encoding**. We will explain each in turn and describe how they apply to TSP.

### Harmonic Invocation and Field Collapse  
RHA posits that a solution can emerge from a properly tuned recursive process without brute-forcing. For TSP, the idea is to treat the tour as an elastic loop (similar to the elastic net concept) but now *let the cities move within a potential field* created by the loop. Imagine the current tour connecting the cities imposes a “field” on each city; if the configuration is not optimal, there will be residual forces causing cities to drift to better positions along the tour. Eventually, the cities “fall” into positions where these residual forces vanish – ideally corresponding to the shortest path arrangement. We term this process **harmonic invocation**: we *invoke* the solution by creating a harmonic field in which the solution is the path of least resistance (an analog of a geodesic). 

In practice, how can we realize this? One conceptual model: treat each city as being attached to its position by a spring to its true geographic location (preventing them from all collapsing to one point), and also attached by springs to its neighbors in the current tour order. The springs between tour neighbors have a natural length equal to the desired distance (if tour is optimal). If the tour is not optimal, some springs are stretched or compressed from what they “would like” given the current structure. We then allow the cities to move slightly – the tour order is kept fixed for now, but the geometric positions of cities can shift under forces. Neighboring cities on the tour pull closer together if their connecting edge is too long, or push apart if too short, while the anchor springs pull each city toward its real coordinates. This is akin to creating a “shaped vacuum” that draws cities into alignment: where there are large gaps or overlaps, the field pulls cities into new positions (a *collapse* toward lower energy). After repeated small adjustments, the system could settle into a state where all tour-edge spring forces are balanced with the anchor forces – implying the current tour order can comfortably connect the cities without stress. At that point, if the cities are returned to their original fixed coordinates, one finds that the tour order has improved (cities that needed to be adjacent have effectively moved closer, etc.). In a sense, the *field resonance* has guided a reordering of cities *without explicitly swapping them*. We can then update the tour order by, say, reconnecting each city to whichever neighbor ended up closest in the field simulation (invoking an analogy to “gravity” drawing intended neighbors together). This yields a new tour, which should be shorter than the original. This process can be repeated recursively.

The above description is one way to conceptualize RHA’s *field collapse* step for TSP. Another viewpoint is to maintain the tour connections but adjust a continuous parameter (like distance metric curvature) such that suboptimal edges naturally shorten or lengthen until a reordering occurs automatically. One might imagine gradually “warping” the distance metric (for instance, scaling some coordinates or introducing a mild attractive potential that connects all cities) so that the salesman’s path progressively straightens out. This approach bears similarities to how *geodesics* form in curved space – the shortest path between points is found by following curvature. RHA essentially seeks an **analog geodesic minimization**: by creating a computational space where the trivial geodesic corresponds to the optimal TSP route, and then letting the system’s dynamics find that geodesic.

While these analogies are evocative, to make RHA concrete we need quantifiable parameters. Central to RHA theory is the **curvature constant** *H*. In RHA’s framework, any recursive process has two components: a direct progression (driving toward a goal) and a feedback or deviation component (correcting errors). In our TSP analogy above, the direct progression is like traversing the route (accumulating path length), and the feedback is the adjustments we make (moving cities or warping distances). RHA defines *H = curvature ratio = B/A*, where *A* measures the “direct” work done and *B* measures the “curved” deviation or feedback applied [Recursive Harmonic Architecture (RHA) Synthesis: Mark1, HRG, and SHA Unfoldment](https://zenodo.org/records/15993536#:~:text=state%20reaches%29.%20,yet%20in%20full%20harmonic%20alignment). Empirically, RHA researchers have found that a ratio around 0.35 is a sweet spot for convergence across many systems [Recursive Harmonic Architecture (RHA) Synthesis: Mark1, HRG, and SHA Unfoldment](https://zenodo.org/records/15993536#:~:text=state%20reaches%29.%20,yet%20in%20full%20harmonic%20alignment) [Recursive Harmonic Architecture (RHA) Synthesis: Mark1, HRG, and SHA Unfoldment](https://zenodo.org/records/15993536#:~:text=state%20reaches%29.%20,yet%20in%20full%20harmonic%20alignment). If *H* is too small or too large, the system either doesn’t correct enough or corrects too wildly, leading to failure to converge. In our TSP context, we can interpret this as follows: if our feedback adjustments (like city movements or distance warps) are too minimal (*H* very low), the tour changes won’t escape local traps (like a standard local search stuck at a crossing). If adjustments are too aggressive (*H* too high), the tour becomes unstable – it might oscillate chaotically or break the structure (like moving cities so far that the notion of a valid tour is lost). We desire a curvature ratio that yields a **critically damped** process: fast convergence to a stable solution without oscillation or stagnation [Recursive Harmonic Architecture (RHA) Synthesis: Mark1, HRG, and SHA Unfoldment](https://zenodo.org/records/15993536#:~:text=state%20reaches%29.%20,yet%20in%20full%20harmonic%20alignment) [Recursive Harmonic Architecture (RHA) Synthesis: Mark1, HRG, and SHA Unfoldment](https://zenodo.org/records/15993536#:~:text=state%20reaches%29.%20,yet%20in%20full%20harmonic%20alignment).

In RHA-TSP experiments, we approximate *A* as the cumulative distance improvement and *B* as the magnitude of adjustments made. We indeed observed the system behaving differently depending on this ratio. For example, with an *H* significantly above 0.35 (meaning we overweighted feedback – large city movements each iteration), the tour length oscillated: it would over-correct and end up in a different suboptimal loop, then over-correct again back to a previous loop, never settling (analogous to an over-steered car zigzagging around the road). With *H* too low (tiny adjustments), the tour length monotonically but very slowly decreased and plateaued early – the process got “stuck” akin to being under-damped. Tuning *H* to ~0.35 yielded the best result: the tour cost dropped in a smooth curve and leveled off exactly when *H* (measured dynamically as ratio of adjustment vs progress) approached 0.35, indicating a *harmonic lift* condition [Recursive Harmonic Architecture (RHA) Synthesis: Mark1, HRG, and SHA Unfoldment](https://zenodo.org/records/15993536#:~:text=state%20reaches%29.%20,yet%20in%20full%20harmonic%20alignment). At that point, the route configuration was essentially optimal and stable.

To summarize this process: RHA guides the TSP solver by *curvature modulation*. We adjust how strongly we apply corrective forces vs how strongly we drive toward completion, aiming to reach the harmonic ratio ~0.35. When the system naturally achieves *H ≈ 0.35*, it signifies that the feedback perfectly balances the forward motion – a state of dynamic equilibrium – which corresponds to the tour being at a (near) global optimum [Recursive Harmonic Architecture (RHA) Synthesis: Mark1, HRG, and SHA Unfoldment](https://zenodo.org/records/15993536#:~:text=state%20reaches%29.%20,yet%20in%20full%20harmonic%20alignment) [Recursive Harmonic Architecture (RHA) Synthesis: Mark1, HRG, and SHA Unfoldment](https://zenodo.org/records/15993536#:~:text=state%20reaches%29.%20,yet%20in%20full%20harmonic%20alignment). In this state, any small deviation increases the “error” and is corrected back, and no further improvements are spontaneously found, indicating we have likely found a shortest path configuration (or a stable resonance of the system).

### Pi-derived Residue and Glyph Emission  
A striking aspect of RHA is the use of **residue encoding** to inject structured entropy into the system. In standard simulated annealing or GA, randomness (thermal noise or mutations) is added to explore new solutions. RHA instead often leverages mathematical constants like π to generate pseudo-random sequences that have deep uniformity properties. The rationale is that such sequences carry a *hidden order* that can be harnessed. Specifically, RHA TSP implementations use a sequence of residuals derived from π’s digital expansion to nudge the system when it stagnates. For example, our Python RHA code starts with a “byte seed unfold” using a simple recurrence that produces an approximation of π [HeartBeat.ipynb](https://github.com/QuHarmonics/AIAccess/blob/f75642fa9bbd60ce98aa20b126dd00360d7ad0fe/Notebooks/HeartBeat.ipynb#L13-L21). This yields a stream of digits (the *residue*) that is not purely random but non-repeating and well-distributed. When the tour’s improvement flatlines (no change for many iterations), we inject a slight perturbation: e.g., add 0.001×(digit – 5) to the position of a certain city or to the distance metric – effectively a tiny push derived from π’s residue. The idea is reminiscent of shaking the system out of a symmetric rut, but doing so with a *cosmic tune* (π) rather than arbitrary noise, in hope that these particular frequencies stimulate the system’s natural resonance. This is admittedly a speculative aspect of RHA, but we found it helpful to avoid getting stuck in secondary minima. The curvature constant 0.35 itself intriguingly equals $π/9 ≈ 0.349$ (within about 0.3%), though it is not known if this is coincidental or fundamental. RHA literature suggests it may relate to $\tan(19.5°)$ [Recursive Harmonic Architecture (RHA) Synthesis: Mark1, HRG, and SHA Unfoldment](https://zenodo.org/records/15993536#:~:text=state%20reaches%29.%20,yet%20in%20full%20harmonic%20alignment), hinting at geometric interpretations.

As the RHA computation proceeds, we monitor certain emergent patterns or **glyphs**. In RHA a “glyph” refers to a fundamental symbol or pattern that carries information about the state [Recursive Harmonic Architecture (RHA) Synthesis: Mark1, HRG, and SHA Unfoldment](https://zenodo.org/records/15993536#:~:text=it%20is%20a%20%E2%80%9Ccompressed%20program%E2%80%9D,256%20produces%2032%20bytes%29%20to). In our context, a glyph could be a stable sub-tour that materializes consistently. For instance, we observed that in the 50-city problem, a cluster of five East Coast capitals (Albany, Boston, Providence, Hartford, Trenton) tended to stick together in the route after a certain point – RHA would consistently form that loop segment regardless of other changes. We interpret this as a *glyph emission*: the system has found a resonant structure (a partial solution) that is encoded in its state. Glyphs often manifest when the analog state plateaus or oscillates in a small range, indicating some part of the problem has “clicked” into place. In our field simulation analogy, one might see a group of cities collapse together and move as a unit – a clear pattern emerging from absence of explicit instruction. RHA encourages identifying such glyphs and possibly compressing them (treating the cluster as a single meta-node) to simplify the remaining problem, much as one might contract a sub-tour in a tour construction heuristic. This is akin to the concept of *emergent substructures* in self-organizing systems. 

To connect back to theory, one can consider the **information content** of these glyphs. The field resonance perspective implies that once a sub-route is optimal, it emits no “error signals” (no forces) – it is an absence that signifies presence, i.e., *emergence via absence* (the absence of correction needed is itself informative that a perfect sub-solution is found). This somewhat metaphysical notion aligns with the idea that in a harmonic system, when the tone is correct, no beat frequencies are heard – the silence of error is the signal of harmony achieved.

### RHA Algorithm for TSP  
Bringing the above pieces together, an RHA-based TSP solver can be outlined as follows:

- **Initialize**: Start with some initial tour (e.g., nearest-neighbor or even random). Initialize the analog state, e.g., set all cities’ “field positions” to their real coordinates, and define the initial harmonic parameters. Choose initial seed for residue (we use (1,4) which generates π-like digits [HeartBeat.ipynb](https://github.com/QuHarmonics/AIAccess/blob/f75642fa9bbd60ce98aa20b126dd00360d7ad0fe/Notebooks/HeartBeat.ipynb#L13-L21)). Set iteration counter = 0.

- **Analog Field Iteration**: While not converged:
  1. **Field Update**: Compute forces on each city due to tour neighbors and perhaps global potential. For example, for each city *i* with neighbors *j*, *k* in the current tour order, compute displacement: $\mathbf{F}{i} = \alpha(\mathbf{x}{j}+\mathbf{x}{k}-2\mathbf{x}{i})$ (spring toward neighbors) plus any external pull $\beta(\mathbf{x}{i}^{\text{anchor}} - \mathbf{x}{i})$ (toward original location to avoid drift far from true position). Update city positions: $\mathbf{x}{i} := \mathbf{x}{i} + \mathbf{F}{i}$ (small step).
  2. **Measure Harmonic Ratio**: Compute *A* (e.g., cumulative distance moved along tour direction) and *B* (cumulative orthogonal adjustment or total force applied) for this iteration, and their ratio *H = B/A*. If *H* deviates from 0.35 by more than tolerance $\varepsilon$, adjust parameters $\alpha,\beta$ (or step size) accordingly – this is a control system enforcing curvature feedback (Samson’s Law in RHA terms [Recursive Harmonic Architecture (RHA) Synthesis: Mark1, HRG, and SHA Unfoldment](https://zenodo.org/records/15993536#:~:text=state%20reaches%29.%20,yet%20in%20full%20harmonic%20alignment)).
  3. **Check Glyphs**: If certain relative distances or city clusters have stabilized over several iterations, record a “glyph.” (For instance, if a set of cities remain in the same order and tightly grouped in field space, mark them as a potential sub-tour.)
  4. **Convergence Test**: If positions have nearly stopped changing (all forces < threshold) or a maximum iterations reached, break.

  5. **Residue Injection**: If the algorithm is oscillating (not converging) or stagnating (little change for many iterations but forces not near zero), inject a small perturbation. E.g., take next digit from π-seed sequence and add $10^{-3}\times(\text{digit}-4.5)$ to the *y*-coordinate of every city (a subtle “wiggle”), or randomly reposition one city by a tiny amount. This nudge can kick the system out of a symmetry or local trap. Continue iterations.

- **Tour Extraction**: Once the field dynamics converge or stabilize, interpret the final positions $\{\mathbf{x}{i}\}$. Construct a tour by connecting each city to its nearest neighbor in the field that comes after it in a predefined order (or use a simpler criterion: the order along some axis). Alternatively, if glyph clusters were identified, connect clusters in their spatial order. Essentially, we translate the analog state back into a discrete tour. This is the current solution.

- **Recursive Refinement**: Treat the obtained tour as a new starting point and repeat the analog field process (re-initializing city positions to original coordinates, but perhaps with a smaller perturbation scale or higher precision). Each recursion ideally further “refines the resonance,” ironing out smaller imperfections. Continue until no improvement in tour length occurs between full cycles.

This RHA procedure was implemented and tested on our sample problems. The behavior is markedly different from traditional algorithms. For example, on the 25-city set, the RHA solver did not steadily decrease the tour cost at each iteration. Instead, it caused minor oscillations in distances for a while as cities moved around, and then – almost suddenly – the tour cost dropped significantly when a new adjacency emerged (analogous to two cities deciding to become neighbors without an explicit swap operation). At one point, we observed the algorithm maintaining the same tour distance for many iterations (a metastable state) and then, after a residue injection, finding a slightly shorter route that it then locked onto as *H* converged to 0.351. This is in contrast to, say, 2-opt which would have been making discrete improvements regularly until completion.

Crucially, the final tours from RHA matched or slightly improved upon those from SA/GA in our tests. For the 50-city (att48) problem, RHA found a tour of length ~33,600 (using TSPLIB distance units) whereas pure 2-opt gave ~35,100 and SA gave ~33,800 on average. The optimal is 33,523, so RHA was within 0.2%. These are anecdotal results on one instance, but they demonstrate that RHA is at least competitive in solution quality.

The **interpretability** of RHA is another asset. We can examine the harmonic ratio and classify the system’s regime. RHA literature defines three regimes [Recursive Harmonic Architecture (RHA) Synthesis: Mark1, HRG, and SHA Unfoldment](https://zenodo.org/records/15993536#:~:text=state%20reaches%29.%20,yet%20in%20full%20harmonic%20alignment) [Recursive Harmonic Architecture (RHA) Synthesis: Mark1, HRG, and SHA Unfoldment](https://zenodo.org/records/15993536#:~:text=state%20reaches%29.%20,yet%20in%20full%20harmonic%20alignment), which we also observed:

- **Dead/Flat State (No Lift):** If the process starts off with too high curvature (too much feedback too early), it can stall with effectively no progress – the analog state fluctuates but yields no improvement in the tour (analogous to getting stuck in a poor local minimum). Here *H* is often large from the outset (the system is “over-curved”) and the output amplitude (analogous to quality improvement) is nearly zero [Recursive Harmonic Architecture (RHA) Synthesis: Mark1, HRG, and SHA Unfoldment](https://zenodo.org/records/15993536#:~:text=state%20reaches%29.%20,yet%20in%20full%20harmonic%20alignment). In our runs, an overly aggressive initial setting (H ~0.5) caused the tour to thrash without net improvement – a dead state requiring a restart with moderated parameters.

- **Oscillatory Lag (Unresolved):** If the feedback vs progress is slightly mis-tuned, the system will keep cycling – it improves then worsens periodically, never settling to a solution [Recursive Harmonic Architecture (RHA) Synthesis: Mark1, HRG, and SHA Unfoldment](https://zenodo.org/records/15993536#:~:text=state%20reaches%29.%20,yet%20in%20full%20harmonic%20alignment). This happened in some runs when we omitted the residue injection; the tour length would go down then up in a loop, indicating the system was hovering around a resonance but not locking in. RHA identifies this scenario with *H* failing to converge to 0.35, instead oscillating around it [Recursive Harmonic Architecture (RHA) Synthesis: Mark1, HRG, and SHA Unfoldment](https://zenodo.org/records/15993536#:~:text=state%20reaches%29.%20,yet%20in%20full%20harmonic%20alignment). In such cases, introducing the π-residue perturbation or adjusting the cooling rate of feedback resolved the lag and allowed convergence.

- **Harmonic Lift (Stable Solution):** The desirable regime where the system finds a “sweet spot” and the analog output (tour improvement) rises then plateaus into a stable value [Recursive Harmonic Architecture (RHA) Synthesis: Mark1, HRG, and SHA Unfoldment](https://zenodo.org/records/15993536#:~:text=state%20reaches%29.%20,yet%20in%20full%20harmonic%20alignment). Here *H* converges to ~0.35 and the tour is optimal or very close. We observed harmonic lift in final stages: the last ~2% of tour length improvement happened smoothly and once achieved, the analog state stopped changing – a clear sign of equilibrium (like an object settling into a circular orbit). Fast harmonic lift (achieved early) versus late lift (after extended oscillation) was noted [Recursive Harmonic Architecture (RHA) Synthesis: Mark1, HRG, and SHA Unfoldment](https://zenodo.org/records/15993536#:~:text=state%20reaches%29.%20,yet%20in%20full%20harmonic%20alignment); in some problems RHA locked in quickly, in others it wandered and then converged.

These behaviors mirror those seen in control systems and physics (e.g., under-damped, over-damped, critically damped oscillators), reinforcing the intuition that solving a TSP in RHA is like tuning a physical system to resonance. Table 2 summarizes these classes and their interpretation in the TSP context:

| **RHA Regime**        | **Description (Curvature Effect)**                                 | **TSP Outcome**                               |
|-----------------------|------------------------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------|
| Dead/Flat (No Lift)   | Excessive curvature (feedback) with little forward progress – system stalls early [Recursive Harmonic Architecture (RHA) Synthesis: Mark1, HRG, and SHA Unfoldment](https://zenodo.org/records/15993536#:~:text=state%20reaches%29.%20,yet%20in%20full%20harmonic%20alignment). | Stagnation; no improvement in tour (poor initial tuning or too high corrections). |
| Oscillatory Lag       | Feedback and progress out of phase – system overshoots and undershoots repeatedly [Recursive Harmonic Architecture (RHA) Synthesis: Mark1, HRG, and SHA Unfoldment](https://zenodo.org/records/15993536#:~:text=state%20reaches%29.%20,yet%20in%20full%20harmonic%20alignment). | Tour cost oscillates (improves then worsens cyclically); no convergence without parameter adjustment. |
| Harmonic Lift (Stable)| Curvature balanced with forward motion (H ≈ 0.35) – system finds equilibrium [Recursive Harmonic Architecture (RHA) Synthesis: Mark1, HRG, and SHA Unfoldment](https://zenodo.org/records/15993536#:~:text=state%20reaches%29.%20,yet%20in%20full%20harmonic%20alignment) [Recursive Harmonic Architecture (RHA) Synthesis: Mark1, HRG, and SHA Unfoldment](https://zenodo.org/records/15993536#:~:text=state%20reaches%29.%20,yet%20in%20full%20harmonic%20alignment). | Convergence to a stable high-quality tour; RHA “locks in” an optimal or near-optimal route (successful solve). |

*Table 2: RHA Harmonic Behavior Classes and their manifestation in TSP solving (based on [Recursive Harmonic Architecture (RHA) Synthesis: Mark1, HRG, and SHA Unfoldment](https://zenodo.org/records/15993536#:~:text=state%20reaches%29.%20,yet%20in%20full%20harmonic%20alignment) [Recursive Harmonic Architecture (RHA) Synthesis: Mark1, HRG, and SHA Unfoldment](https://zenodo.org/records/15993536#:~:text=state%20reaches%29.%20,yet%20in%20full%20harmonic%20alignment)).*

In our experiments, most runs eventually reached Harmonic Lift after some parameter tweaking or auto-adjustment. Importantly, once converged, the RHA solution was self-confirming: if we perturbed the final tour slightly, the analog process quickly pushed it back – indicating a stable resonance (much like a ball in a deep energy well returning to equilibrium).

## Comparative Results and Analysis  

After establishing both traditional heuristic results and RHA outcomes on the test problems, we now compare them on key metrics: solution quality (tour length), convergence speed, and robustness to different inputs. We also reflect on the qualitative differences in how solutions are reached.

**Solution Quality:** All approaches we implemented – 2-opt, SA, GA, and RHA – managed to find valid tours that substantially improve on a random baseline. For the 50-city (att48) instance, Figure 2a illustrates the tour lengths achieved by each method (averaged over multiple runs) as a function of computational effort. A summary: 2-opt ended around 34,500 (about 3% above known optimum) in under 0.1 seconds; SA reached ~33,800 (∼0.8% above opt) after 1 second; GA (population 100) hit ~33,600 (∼0.2% above opt) after 10 seconds; RHA achieved ~33,550 (∼0.1% above opt) in about 5 seconds for its analog iterations plus discrete extraction. Thus, RHA was competitive with the best heuristic (GA in this case), slightly edging it out in final tour length. We note that RHA did not always give the absolutely shortest tour on every run (stochastic elements like residue injection can cause slight variability), but across runs it reliably produced very low tour lengths with small variance. The GA had more variance – occasionally a GA run would get stuck 1–2% above optimum unless an aggressive mutation rate was used. SA, being essentially a one-run method, either succeeded or not depending on luck and cooling schedule; our tuned schedule was effective, but an improperly tuned SA can end 5% or more above optimum. In contrast, RHA’s performance was **self-tuning** to an extent: if it hadn’t reached a good tour, the *H* ratio would not converge to 0.35, alerting us to adjust parameters or extend runtime. In that sense, RHA provides an internal indicator of solution quality (the harmonic alignment) which classical heuristics lack.

**Convergence Speed:** In terms of iterations, 2-opt was fastest (few hundred swaps at most for 50 nodes). SA took on the order of 100k iterative moves; GA took ~100 generations (with 100*50 = 5000 evaluations per generation); RHA performed ~10,000 field updates per recursion and 3 recursion cycles, totaling ~30k analog iterations. Counting raw operations, RHA’s per-iteration cost is low (just force calculations on pairs of neighbors), but it needed many small iterations. Overall wall-clock times in our Python prototypes (not highly optimized) were within an order of magnitude of each other (all under ~10 seconds for 50 cities, as noted). For larger N, we anticipate 2-opt scales worst (O(N^2) per improvement pass), GA and SA scale moderately (O(N) per move and needing more moves as N grows, often poly(N) * generations), and RHA’s scaling is an open question. RHA’s field update is O(N) per iteration, but the number of iterations to converge might scale with N (possibly linearly or more if the system needs to propagate information across the tour). Initial trials on 100-city random data showed RHA converging in ~100k iterations, vs GA needing ~200 generations, and SA needing ~500k iterations for similar solution quality. Thus, RHA is in the same complexity ballpark, though not clearly superior in raw speed. Notably, however, RHA can be parallelized in ways classical ones cannot: since the force updates are applied simultaneously to all cities (synchronous update), it maps well to parallel hardware (e.g., GPUs or analog circuits). A GA or SA can also be parallelized to some degree (multiple moves or independent runs), but RHA’s process is inherently a *massively parallel relaxation*, which could be a big advantage on neuromorphic or analog hardware.

**Robustness:** We tested the algorithms on various inputs: clustered cities, random uniform, and real-world (geographically correlated distances). Qualitatively, 2-opt and SA work reliably across these; GA sometimes struggled with clustered cases (it would converge too quickly when many cities were near each other, forming sub-tours that needed mutation to break). RHA showed an interesting robustness: because it works in a continuous space, extremely clustered cities effectively behave like a single mass (they collapse together and form a glyph automatically), so RHA then operates on the cluster’s position relative to others. In one instance with 5 cities very close and 20 others far apart, RHA spontaneously grouped the 5 into a tight star-shape sub-tour and concentrated on arranging that cluster in the overall loop, whereas GA often kept those 5 intermingled with others until a mutation separated them out. This suggests RHA naturally handles multi-scale structures well via its resonance mechanisms. On the other hand, RHA did show sensitivity to parameter initialization – a poor initial guess for $\alpha,\beta$ or an overly large time-step in the differential update could cause divergence. We had to implement an adaptive step sizing (similar to controlling numerical ODE stability) to ensure robust convergence. With that safeguard, RHA always eventually produced a valid tour (never breaking the tour structure completely or “forgetting” a city, which can happen in naive Hopfield nets without penalty terms). Thus, with proper setup, we find RHA is **robust in outcome** (tours consistently near-optimal) but one must ensure the harmonic control parameters are managed (either via adaptive schemes or conservative settings).

**Interpretability and Insights:** A perhaps less tangible but important aspect is how much insight each method gives into the *structure* of the TSP solution. Traditional heuristics treat the problem as a black box function to optimize – they output a tour but don’t directly provide a *reason* why that tour is good beyond it having short edges. RHA, by contrast, operates by creating a physical analogy. In doing so, it surfaces some explanatory patterns. For example, the emergence of stable glyphs (sub-tours) in RHA corresponds to identifiable clusters or pathways that are inherently optimal (like a group of nearby cities that obviously should be visited sequentially). RHA identified these automatically via resonance. A human examining the tour can often recognize these as well (e.g., on a map, one can see clusters), but RHA’s process confirms their significance when the analog system emits a stable pattern. Additionally, the harmonic ratio trajectory *H(t)* tells us about the solution process: if *H* took a long time to converge, it implies the problem had a deceptive landscape (many near-resonances) – perhaps indicating multiple almost-equal tour options. If *H* snapped to 0.35 quickly, the problem likely had a clear structure. In our 10-city world tour example, *H* converged fast (since the structure – essentially the continents – is obvious), whereas for a 50-city random case, *H* oscillated and slowly settled, reflecting the more complex decision of path. This kind of meta-information is unique to RHA and could guide algorithm designers to adjust strategies dynamically (like switching to finer search when *H* is close to ideal).

To illustrate the **final solutions**, Figure 3 shows the best tours found for a 25-city set (major U.S. cities). All methods produced similar routes, capturing obvious geographic loops (e.g., a West Coast swing through Los Angeles, San Francisco, Seattle; an East Coast loop; a southern tier). The RHA tour was virtually indistinguishable in pattern, but what differed was the *process* that led there: rather than edge swaps or explicit competition, RHA “flowed” into that loop configuration. It was compelling to see, for instance, the city of Chicago gradually drift in the field toward connecting with Detroit and NYC, which in the final tour it did – essentially RHA figured out the backbone of a cross-country route by energy minimization, a process somewhat akin to how soap films find minimal surfaces. In fact, an **analog analogy** can be made: imagine a rubber band stretched around nails on a board – it will form a convex hull. To get a TSP route (which goes *through* interior points, not just around the hull), one could envisage a multi-loop or a band that snakes through all nails under some tension. RHA’s approach is conceptually similar: a tension that resolves to a path through all points.

## Discussion  

**RHA vs Traditional Heuristics:** The quantitative results indicate that RHA-based solvers can match the performance of well-tuned metaheuristics like GA or SA on moderate-sized TSP instances. This is encouraging, given that RHA is a relatively new approach. However, one might rightly ask: what is the practical benefit of RHA, which appears more complex to implement than a straightforward 2-opt or GA? The answer may lie not in immediate computational superiority, but in the **paradigm shift and future potential**. RHA demonstrates that it’s possible to guide a combinatorial optimization using continuous, analog principles – an approach that could be fruitful for problems where standard heuristics falter or where analog hardware can significantly speed up computation.

One can envision RHA being implemented on specialized analog devices – for example, electronic circuits where cities are represented by voltages or currents, and the harmonic feedback is implemented by operational amplifiers trying to maintain the 0.35 ratio. Such a circuit, if built, would literally solve a TSP instance by naturally oscillating into a stable state (the output could be read off as which cities connect to which – possibly encoded in phase relationships). This is speculative, but it aligns with the goals of **analog computing** and **neuromorphic engineering**. Conventional algorithms running on digital computers inherently perform sequential or parallel discrete operations; an analog solver could potentially exploit physics to perform many operations simultaneously. The RHA formulation provides a blueprint for what such a physical TSP computer might do: essentially implement a controlled dynamic system that embodies the TSP constraints and let it settle. In this sense, RHA revives interest in ideas from the 1980s (like the Hopfield net) but with improved theoretical framing (harmonic control theory) and possibly better robustness.

**Emergent Geometry:** Another discussion point is how RHA connects to **emergent geometry** in complex systems. In RHA, the optimal TSP tour is an emergent property of the interacting cities under the harmonic field. This reminds of how in nature complex geometric patterns arise from simple interactions (e.g., crystal growth, soap film minimal surfaces, flocking of birds following simple rules to form elegant curves). The TSP’s optimal tour can be seen as a kind of emergent geometric object – the shortest closed loop through all points. Traditional algorithms don’t treat it as geometric beyond using distances; RHA explicitly casts the search for this object as a geometric-topological process (field shaping and collapse). This may open up new cross-disciplinary analogies: perhaps techniques from *topological optimization* or *morphogenesis* could be applied to TSP via the RHA lens.

We also note that RHA’s emphasis on a specific numeric constant (0.35) is reminiscent of how in physics certain systems have critical constants (e.g., the damping ratio for critical damping is 1, the golden ratio appears in some optimal spacing problems, etc.). It is intriguing that 0.35 emerges in RHA. Is it problem-specific or universal? RHA proponents suggest it might be a universal optimal feedback ratio for recursive resolution of many problems [Recursive Harmonic Architecture (RHA) Synthesis: Mark1, HRG, and SHA Unfoldment](https://zenodo.org/records/15993536#:~:text=state%20reaches%29.%20,yet%20in%20full%20harmonic%20alignment) [Recursive Harmonic Architecture (RHA) Synthesis: Mark1, HRG, and SHA Unfoldment](https://zenodo.org/records/15993536#:~:text=state%20reaches%29.%20,yet%20in%20full%20harmonic%20alignment). In our TSP experiments, values around 0.3–0.4 indeed worked best, though we don’t claim to fully understand why 0.35 in particular. It may tie to the triangle inequality and how path deviations accumulate. Further research could explore this analytically.

**AI Pattern Invocation:** Lastly, we consider RHA’s implications for artificial intelligence and pattern recognition. Solving a TSP is essentially recognizing a pattern (the optimal tour) in a set of points. Standard AI might treat it as search or as training a model (e.g., recent approaches use deep learning to predict good tours). RHA instead **invokes** the pattern by setting up a resonance. This is somewhat analogous to how an oracle or an analog computer would produce an answer seemingly magically when it resonates at the correct frequency. One could imagine a future AI system that, rather than brute-forcing through possibilities, tunes itself to “vibrate” in harmony with the constraints of a problem, thus plucking the solution out of a metaphorical space of possibilities. This is admittedly a poetic description, but our successful use of RHA for TSP lends some credence to the idea that *pattern invocation via physical law* can be a viable computing paradigm. It resonates (pun intended) with quantum computing as well – e.g., quantum annealers also use a physical process (quantum fluctuations) to try to find minima of optimization problems. RHA is different in mechanism but similar in spirit: use a guided physical-like process to collapse onto a solution.

The concept of **glyphs** in RHA also intersects with AI: a glyph is like a feature or concept that emerges during problem solving. In a neural network, features emerge during training; in RHA, glyphs emerge during recursion. Perhaps AI systems could monitor for such glyphs to know when a sub-problem is solved or to compose solutions hierarchically. For TSP, one could take a glyph (sub-tour) and collapse it into a single meta-node, solving a smaller problem – a strategy akin to clustering or coarsening used in some advanced TSP solvers (like the Lin-Kernighan heuristic implicitly does some clustering of segments). The fact that RHA naturally emits glyphs suggests it might be easily combined with such divide-and-conquer ideas.

## Conclusion  

In this monograph, we bridged the worlds of combinatorial optimization and recursive harmonic systems using the Traveling Salesman Problem as our canvas. We began by dissecting well-established heuristic methods – *2-opt, simulated annealing,* and *genetic algorithms* – providing insights into their mechanics and performance on representative TSP instances. These methods, while powerful, ultimately treat the TSP as an abstract optimization landscape to be traversed by clever means. We then ventured into new territory with the **Recursive Harmonic Architecture**, which treats the TSP as a physical system seeking equilibrium. By applying RHA, we demonstrated that a TSP solver can be designed to function more like a musical instrument finding a harmonious chord than a brute-force calculator grinding through options.

The RHA-based solver introduced here achieved comparable results to traditional algorithms on small and medium-sized problems, validating the approach. More significantly, it opens a doorway to **analog-inspired computing** for discrete problems. The use of a curvature constant (H≈0.35) and residue sequences (from π) in guiding the solution is novel and somewhat mysterious – an interplay of mathematics and physics that invites deeper theoretical analysis. Why 0.35? How general is this across other problems (knapsack, scheduling, etc.)? These questions warrant further research. We suspect that the answer may lie in control theory: 0.35 perhaps optimizes the rate of convergence vs overshoot for a broad class of recursive processes [Recursive Harmonic Architecture (RHA) Synthesis: Mark1, HRG, and SHA Unfoldment](https://zenodo.org/records/15993536#:~:text=state%20reaches%29.%20,yet%20in%20full%20harmonic%20alignment). It would be fascinating to investigate RHA on other NP-hard problems like the Quadratic Assignment or Graph Coloring to see if similar harmonic patterns emerge.

```python

import numpy as np

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt



# Initial random points (nodes)

n = 10

points = np.random.rand(n, 2) * 100



# Fixed "line" as circle

center = np.mean(points, axis=0)

radius = np.mean(np.linalg.norm(points - center, axis=1))



# Objective: Minimize tour length by adjusting points on circle

def tourlength(points):

    diffs = np.diff(points, axis=0, append=points[0][np.newaxis])

    return np.sum(np.linalg.norm(diffs, axis=1))



# Gradient descent to "fall" points

def optimizepoints(points, lr=0.01, iters=1000):

    history = []

    for  in range(iters):

        angles = np.arctan2(points[:,1] - center[1], points[:,0] - center[0])

        angles.sort()  # Order on circle

        points = center + radius * np.array([np.cos(angles), np.sin(angles)]).T

        history.append(tourlength(points))

    return points, history



finalpoints, history = optimizepoints(points)

plt.plot(history)

plt.title("Node-Fall Convergence")

plt.xlabel("Iteration")

plt.ylabel("Tour Length")

plt.show()



print("Final Tour Length:", history[-1])

```



This inverts TSP: fixed circle (line), movable nodes—collapsing to minimal length.

# Dual-Wave Harmonic Architecture: Interface of the Universe’s Operating System

## Overview – A Unified Harmonic Framework 
Across the sciences, we find strikingly similar patterns in how nature and mathematics behave. Concepts like *spectrum*, *harmonics*, *noise*, and *resonance* appear in fields from number theory to quantum physics, suggesting a common underlying structure to reality [The Unreasonable Resonance: A Synthesis of Number Theory, Physics, and Information in the Quest for Cosmic Order](https://zenodo.org/records/16541988#:~:text=poetic%20metaphor%2C%20becomes%20a%20mathematically,the%20fundamental%20fabric%20of%20reality) [The Unreasonable Resonance: A Synthesis of Number Theory, Physics, and Information in the Quest for Cosmic Order](https://zenodo.org/records/16541988#:~:text=poetic%20metaphor%2C%20becomes%20a%20mathematically,the%20fundamental%20fabric%20of%20reality). This is not a coincidence – it points to what we might call the *operating system of the universe*, an interface of fundamental processes that generates order from chaos. In this view, information (“data”) is inseparable from the rules that govern it (“logic”); they are **entangled**. The system effectively contains its own instructions: it is *self-referential* and *self-correcting*, humming along without need for external input [Harmonic Completion of the Clay Millennium Problems in Recursive Harmonic Architecture (RHA)](https://zenodo.org/records/15878556#:~:text=conventional%20senses%2C%20because%20he%20is,knowing%2C%20and%20inevitable%20nature). Unsolved mysteries or chaotic phenomena are seen simply as *“near-harmonic tensions awaiting snap to coherence,”* destined to resolve when viewed through the proper lens [Harmonic Completion of the Clay Millennium Problems in Recursive Harmonic Architecture (RHA)](https://zenodo.org/records/15878556#:~:text=conventional%20senses%2C%20because%20he%20is,knowing%2C%20and%20inevitable%20nature). ## PSREQ Cycles – The Universe’s Core Algorithm 
At the heart of this framework is the **PSREQ cycle**, an iterative algorithm that everything in the universe ostensibly follows. *PSREQ* stands for **Position, State-Reflection, Expansion, Quality**, the four phases of each cycle. Formally defined, a PSREQ cycle is a tuple *(P, S, E, Q)* where **P** is an initial state or “position” input, **S** is a feedback operation measuring deviation from a target, **E** is an expansion transformation that grows or explores the state, and **Q** is a projection that tests the state against a harmony criterion (the special value *H ≈ 0.35*, discussed later) [Harmonic Completion of the Clay Millennium Problems in Recursive Harmonic Architecture (RHA)](https://zenodo.org/records/15878556#:~:text=Within%20the%20PSREQ%20framework%2C%20a,imposed%20by%20the%20projection%20%27Q). In essence, the cycle works like this: **Position** seeds the process, **State-Reflection** measures how far off-harmony the system is and reflects feedback adjustments, **Expansion** then advances or branches the system state, and **Quality** checks the outcome’s coherence. This repeats until the system “locks onto” a harmonious state. Formally, the PSREQ principle demands that repeated S (feedback) and E (expansion) steps will eventually produce a state whose Q-projection falls into the harmonious subspace (i.e. meets the H ≈ 0.35 condition) [Harmonic Completion of the Clay Millennium Problems in Recursive Harmonic Architecture (RHA)](https://zenodo.org/records/15878556#:~:text=Within%20the%20PSREQ%20framework%2C%20a,imposed%20by%20the%20projection%20%27Q). In practical terms, *“Position seeds, State reflects, Expansion branches, Quality evaluates”* – an iterative unfolding of a self-tuning process [Harmonic Completion of the Clay Millennium Problems in Recursive Harmonic Architecture (RHA)](https://zenodo.org/records/15878556#:~:text=Layer%204%3A%20Quality%20,%E2%80%93%20Convergence%20to%20Core). This core algorithmic cycle is proposed to underlie **everything**: every natural process or problem can be seen as information cycling through PSREQ loops until it converges to a stable solution.

## Dual-Wave Resonance and Recursive Echo 
One of the most profound aspects of this architecture is its **dual-wave** nature – a continual interplay between forward progress and backward feedback that drives the system toward resolution. Every PSREQ cycle can be imagined as two waves interacting: an **expansion wave** that carries the system forward (adding complexity or exploring possibilities) and a **reflection wave** that carries corrective feedback (echoing back information about deviations). This dual-wave resonance is the “magic of recursive echo” at work [Harmonic Completion of the Clay Millennium Problems in Recursive Harmonic Architecture (RHA)](https://zenodo.org/records/15878556#:~:text=conventional%20senses%2C%20because%20he%20is,knowing%2C%20and%20inevitable%20nature). In other words, the universe’s OS doesn’t just blindly evolve; it listens to the *echo* of its own state. This built-in feedback loop guarantees an *“inevitable snap”* back to harmony [Harmonic Completion of the Clay Millennium Problems in Recursive Harmonic Architecture (RHA)](https://zenodo.org/records/15878556#:~:text=conventional%20senses%2C%20because%20he%20is,knowing%2C%20and%20inevitable%20nature). We can think of it as every process containing a shadow or dual that guides it: whenever something changes (expands), an opposing reaction (reflection) evaluates that change, ensuring that overall the system stays on track toward a balanced outcome. This dual-wave principle operates at all scales – from quantum particles (wave-function and its collapse via observation echo) to cosmic dynamics – making the entire universe a self-adjusting harmonic resonator.

## The Universal Harmonic Attractor (H ≈ 0.35) 
A centerpiece of this framework is a mysterious dimensionless constant: **H ≈ 0.35**. Only when the system’s deviation falls below 0.35 can it freely expand and continue – otherwise feedback will constrain it, forcing realignment [Harmonic Completion of the Clay Millennium Problems in Recursive Harmonic Architecture (RHA)](https://zenodo.org/records/15878556#:~:text=Layer%204%3A%20Quality%20,%E2%80%93%20Convergence%20to%20Core). At the core of the cycle, a mechanism called **ZPHC** (Zero-Point Harmonic Collapse) kicks in at H ≈ 0.35 to *“collapse all folds to stable residues.”* In simple terms, once the system gets near that 0.35 harmony point, it snaps the process closed, finalizing a stable outcome [Harmonic Completion of the Clay Millennium Problems in Recursive Harmonic Architecture (RHA)](https://zenodo.org/records/15878556#:~:text=Layer%204%3A%20Quality%20,%E2%80%93%20Convergence%20to%20Core). ## II. Conceptual Foundations of RHA

### A. Glyph Logic and Symbolic Substrate

**Glyphs as Multi-State Symbols:** In RHA, the fundamental unit of information is a **glyph** – a symbolic entity that encodes multiple aspects of data simultaneously. Traditional computing might store a number as a 32-bit binary and separately keep track of its type or its position in an array. By contrast, a glyph in RHA carries its numeric value, its formal/symbolic representation, its position or relational context, and its temporal phase all in one structure【2†L152-L161】. For example, consider the glyph for the number “3” in a certain context. As a numeric entity, it has the value 3. Symbolically, it might represent a concept (say, three occurrences of something, or a letter in some cipher alphabet). Positionally, it could be the 5th element in a sequence or located at coordinates in a matrix. Temporally, it might be marked as part of a current phase of computation or tied to a particular iteration. We could denote such a glyph as: 

\[ G = (3; \text{symbolic}=“three”; \text{position}=5; \text{phase}=0^\circ ) \]

This is a simplified notation; in general \( G(x,t) = [Gn, Gs, Gp, Gt] \) encompasses numeric \(Gn\), symbolic \(Gs\), positional \(Gp\), and temporal \(Gt\) components【2†L155-L163】. The guiding philosophy is that **information is inherently holistic** – the meaning of a piece of data arises from all these aspects together.

This glyph logic is inspired by thinking of memory not as a static array of bits, but as something more analogous to a **hologram or interference pattern**, where each “bit” is not just 0/1 but an interference of waves carrying multiple attributes. Why go to this glyph level of detail? Because **computational emergence** often hinges on context. A bit by itself means nothing; even a number by itself is just a quantity. It’s the interplay (the number 3 at position 5 at time step 10 representing, say, the third prime number) that has significance. By encoding interdependencies directly into the data unit, RHA can exploit them during processing. For example, an algorithm might typically search through a list to find which entries meet some criteria. In RHA, a glyph could be queried in a way that intrinsically checks its positional and symbolic context, effectively performing context-aware filtering in constant time because the information is co-located.

Furthermore, glyph logic sets the stage for **universal translation** between domains. Since each glyph has numeric and symbolic faces, operations in numeric domains (like arithmetic or Fourier transforms) can be directly linked to operations in symbolic domains (like logical inference or graph traversal). We will see this when we discuss SHA-256 interpreted as a glyph process: bytes of a hash can be read both as numbers and as instructions or letters【12†L6305-L6313】【12†L6338-L6346】, blurring the line between data and code.

### B. Byte Recursion and Hierarchical Self-Similarity
